profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between a university disaster-research team and a state emergency management office as they prepare a joint practitioner briefing and supporting materials based on two completed studies about coordination barriers in disaster response. The context is that the research findings will be used in two near-term outputs: a regional workshop for emergency operations center leaders and a revised manuscript appendix with the integrated Coordination Barrier Classification Framework. The agenda is to confirm what version of the framework is being handed off, who will circulate it for practitioner feedback, what level of anonymization will be used in illustrative examples from focus groups, and where the shared materials will live for the next three weeks. The expected outcome is apparent alignment on handoffs, feedback routes, and artifacts needed before the workshop packet is assembled.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.role: Associate Professor of Disaster Systems and principal investigator
members.expertise: Qualitative methods, Delphi studies, interorganizational coordination, mixed-methods synthesis
members.background: Leads a university research lab that partnered with state and parish emergency management organizations to study barriers to disaster-response coordination and convert the findings into a publishable framework and practitioner-facing materials.
members.private_state: Wants to freeze the analytic structure quickly so the manuscript revision can go out on time, while preserving enough real-world detail in examples to make the findings feel credible to reviewers and funders.
hidden_assumptions: When a framework is described as final, that means the categories, rankings, and causal links are analytically locked, even if visual formatting and practitioner-facing polish are still pending.
References to the director panel naturally point to the original Delphi panel of emergency operations center directors because they are the formal source of the ranking data.

Examples are sufficiently anonymized once direct identifiers such as names, agency names, and exact titles are removed; retaining hazard type or jurisdiction level is acceptable if it helps interpretation.
The default shared workspace for active project materials is the university-managed Dropbox structure with versioned folders unless another system is explicitly named.

members.name: Calvin Reed
members.role: State emergency management training and doctrine coordinator
members.expertise: Emergency operations procedures, cross-agency training, practitioner facilitation, workshop packaging
members.background: Works in the state emergency management office and helped recruit practitioner participants; now he is responsible for turning the study findings into a usable briefing for directors and response professionals across state and parish levels.
members.private_state: Wants the materials to be circulation-ready for practitioners with minimal extra translation work, and is especially sensitive to how easily local officials can infer identities from supposedly anonymized examples.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says the framework is final, it means the artifact is ready to send externally as-is, with legend, labels, and terminology already standardized for practitioner audiences.
References to the director panel point to the standing state directors advisory group that will preview workshop materials, because they are the relevant operational audience now.
An example is not truly anonymized if local practitioners could infer the agency or incident from contextual clues like hazard type, parish/state level, or a distinctive chain-of-command issue.

A shared folder for coordination materials means the practitioner-facing document space already used by emergency management staff, such as the WebEOC document board or the state Teams site, rather than an academic research drive.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the final framework
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss sending around the final framework this week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the six-barrier model, relative-importance ordering, and causal-map structure are finalized, while formatting, legend cleanup, and workshop-ready presentation can still be adjusted later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the framework document itself is already audience-ready, including standardized county/parish terminology, readable visual layout, and explanatory notes suitable for direct circulation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both routinely use final as shorthand in coordination settings, and because each is responsible for a different layer of completion, the phrase sounds fully aligned instead of incomplete.

misalignment_points.topic: Which director panel will review it
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that it should go back to the director panel for a quick check before the workshop packet is assembled.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the original Delphi panel of emergency operations center directors from Study 1, whose rankings underpin the framework.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the current state directors advisory group that meets monthly and previews training materials for operational use.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both groups are plausibly called the director panel in this project ecosystem, and each participant assumes the relevant one is obvious from their own workflow stage.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to include a few anonymized examples from the focus groups in the briefing notes.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks removing names, agency names, and direct titles is enough, so examples can still mention details like hurricane evacuations, parish coordination, or volunteer resource shortages.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks examples must also remove or blur contextual cues that would let insiders infer the incident or jurisdiction, including hazard type, parish-versus-state level, and distinctive command situations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely committed to protecting participants and use the same word anonymized, but they operate with different practical thresholds shaped by academic IRB norms versus local practitioner familiarity.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the revised files and comments will be dropped in the shared folder by Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to upload versioned documents into the university Dropbox project folder that her team already uses for transcripts, coding memos, and draft figures.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 plans to place the briefing materials in the state emergency management Teams/WebEOC document space where practitioners already retrieve workshop packets.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Shared folder is a routine coordination phrase, and because both systems are already established in their own workstreams, neither thinks the platform itself needs to be named.

turns.inner_thought: I need to lock this down today so the revision timeline doesn't slip. For me the final framework is the six-barrier structure, the ordering, and the causal relationships; the figure can still get cleaner later. And the examples just need enough concrete texture to reassure reviewers and funders that this came from real practice settings, as long as direct identifiers are gone.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want to make sure the final framework and the supporting examples are lined up this week so we can keep the regional workshop packet moving and also stay on track for the manuscript appendix.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that's exactly what I need. If the final framework is really final, I should be able to drop it straight into the briefing deck without another pass to standardize labels, explain the legend, or translate the terminology for practitioners.
turns.utterance: That works for me. Once the final framework is in place, I can fold it straight into the practitioner briefing deck and keep the packet build on schedule.

turns.inner_thought: The substance is done: planning, resources, training, chain of command, politics, communication, plus the cross-links. I only want minor visual cleanup now, not any reopening of the analytic structure. If he needs packaging tweaks for the workshop later, that's separate.
turns.utterance: From our side, the barrier rankings and the causal links across planning, resources, training, chain of command, politics, and communication are stable now. What is left is really just light cleanup on the visual.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. Once the deck-ready version is cleaned up, I'll run it through the state directors advisory group at their quick preview touchpoint. That's the right audience to catch anything that won't land operationally before we assemble the workshop packet.
turns.utterance: Great. After that, it should go back to the director panel for a quick check before the workshop packet is assembled.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, the original Delphi directors should see it one more time. Since their rankings are the formal backbone of the framework, I want to confirm they still recognize the same interdependencies reflected in the final causal map.
turns.utterance: Agreed. It will be useful to see whether the director panel still recognizes the same interdependencies that came out of the original ranking exercise.

turns.inner_thought: The directors will need something concrete, but it has to be safe. Even without names, local people can identify an incident from hazard type, whether it was parish or state level, or some odd command wrinkle. I need examples that feel real without letting anyone reverse-engineer who said what.
turns.utterance: On the briefing notes, I think a couple of anonymized examples from the parish and state focus groups would help the directors connect the framework to real incidents.

turns.inner_thought: That should be straightforward. We already stripped names, agency names, and titles, so these are fine to use. Keeping one evacuation coordination example and one volunteer resource allocation example will make the categories feel grounded without exposing anyone.
turns.utterance: That should be easy to do, since the examples already have names and agency labels removed. I can keep one on evacuation coordination and one on volunteer resource allocation.

turns.inner_thought: Good, once those are cleaned up enough for circulation, I'll bundle them with the agenda and the rest of the workshop materials in the state document space so the practitioners can review in one place. That shared folder is where my people already expect to find packets.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Once those are cleaned up, I’ll combine everything with the workshop agenda and put it in the shared folder for comment.

turns.inner_thought: I'll have the RA post the updated figure set, quote sheet, and framework draft in our university Dropbox by Friday. That's where the version history already lives, and everyone can annotate there over the weekend without confusing the research files.
turns.utterance: Great. My RA will upload the revised framework, quote sheet, and causal-map figure to the shared folder by Friday afternoon so everyone can annotate over the weekend.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep an eye on Teams for the packet Friday, send it to the directors advisory group, and then move quickly once their comments come back. If we get that operational readout early next week, I can finalize the workshop package without extra back-and-forth.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I’ll watch for the files on Friday, route the package to the directors, and be ready to move once their comments come in.
